findings.summary: THE GUARD AND THE TIMER ARE COMPUTED FROM DIFFERENT QUANTITIES, so the one input class the guard exists to reject gets through. `sleepFor` validates the `Duration` (`interval.isNegative() || interval.isZero()`, line 79) but the window it returns sleeps `interval.toMillis()` (lines 86-87), which truncates to 0 for EVERY duration in the open range (0 ms, 1 ms). `new BatchingSequencer(delegate, Duration.ofNanos(500_000))` therefore passes a check whose message reads "commitBatchInterval must be positive" and installs `Thread.sleep(0)` -- a zero-length window, which is verbatim the state the comment three lines above says must not be reachable: "A zero interval is not 'batch nothing', it is 'close the window before anyone else can join', which restores the per-pod PUT rate this class exists to remove -- silently, and only under load." With the window at zero the batch degenerates to whatever happens to have queued during the PREVIOUS conditional PUT, so the commit rate becomes 1/PUT-latency instead of 1/commitBatchInterval and rises with both fleet size and store speed -- a rate scaling with pods, which non-negotiable 6 and M4 SPEC acceptance criterion 9 forbid by name. Nothing else in the tree can catch it: `aZeroIntervalIsRefusedBecauseItSilentlyRestoresThePerPodRate` (BatchingSequencerTest.java:283) tests only `Duration.ZERO`, and every criterion-9 test uses the `WindowTimer` seam, never the shipping constructor. The fix is one line -- validate what the timer will actually use (`interval.toMillis() < 1`), or sleep at nanosecond resolution -- and it belongs with the guard rather than in M4.7c, because the guard is what this diff adds.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED in a copy of the staged tree (probe deleted afterwards). A delegate modelling one real conditional PUT at 20 ms; six pods each committing 40 times a second for 2 s -- the fleet AC9 names. Control at `Duration.ofMillis(250)`, the documented default: 7 commit-chain PUTs. Same fixture at `Duration.ofNanos(500_000)`: 98 commit-chain PUTs. A 14x commit-rate regression, with no exception, no log line, and the whole suite green -- the cost model prices this dimension at $52/month at 4 PUT/s, so an operator who tunes `commitBatchInterval` below one millisecond for latency gets roughly $1,200/month and no signal that the batcher stopped batching. The guard reports the configuration as accepted, which is the specific outcome its own comment says would be 'silent, and only under load'.

findings.summary: THE EXIT `close` NEVER REACHES IS INVISIBLE TO AN OPERATOR AND MISREPORTED TO CALLERS. The comment at 174-182 names this path exactly -- "the committer dying on its own -- a timer throw, an Error -- on a live pod with no `close` in sight" -- and the `finally` handles only the callers' futures: `stop()` plus `failAll(drainRemaining(), ...)`. Three things are then wrong at once. (1) NOTHING IS LOGGED, at any level, although `close()` twenty lines below emits a WARNING for the strictly milder case of a join that timed out; the cause reaches exactly one caller -- whichever happened to hold the window -- and is discarded everywhere else. (2) THE MESSAGE IS FALSE: every subsequent caller gets `IOException("this sequencer is closed and must not commit again")` from submit (line 134), the SAME string a real `close()` produces, so an operator debugging a total ingest stall is told to look for a shutdown that never happened and has no way to tell the two apart. (3) THE DELEGATE IS NEVER CLOSED, so a `LocalSequencer` delegate keeps `closed == false` and never calls `leases.release()` (LocalSequencer.java:161-164): the pod holds a lease it can no longer commit through, and a successor must wait out the TTL -- ADR-0007's ~10 s, precisely the failover `Sequencer.close()`'s javadoc (Sequencer.java:113-118) says close exists to avoid, and unbounded rather than TTL-bounded once a renewer thread lands (none exists today; nothing calls `LeaseManager.renew()` outside tests). The class's own reasoning makes this path realistic rather than theoretical: line 165-167 argues the Error case is the batched path itself ('batching exists to make batches big, and CommitLog encodes the delta TWICE per attempt'), and lines 204-206 argue the interrupt case is the textbook store idiom ('which BoundedLock already uses and any S3 backend will use for ClosedByInterruptException'). Failing closed is a defensible choice; failing closed in silence, under a message that says something untrue, is not. Minimum remedy: log the terminating cause at ERROR from the `finally`, and make the refusal name the real reason rather than reusing close's string.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED in a copy of the staged tree, twice (probes deleted afterwards). (a) Delegate whose `commitAll` throws `new OutOfMemoryError("delta encode")`, timer `() -> { }`, and NO close() ever called: first caller receives the OutOfMemoryError; second caller receives `java.io.IOException: this sequencer is closed and must not commit again`; the delegate's `close()` was never invoked (`delegateClosed=false`); nothing printed to stdout or stderr by the class. (b) Delegate that fails ONE commit with the textbook idiom the class's own comment names -- `Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new IOException("store was unreachable")` -- and succeeds thereafter: the first caller correctly gets `IOException: store was unreachable`; the committer then re-enters `queue.take()` with the flag set, dies, and EVERY later caller gets `IOException: this sequencer is closed and must not commit again` forever, with `delegateClosed=false`. In production that is a leaseholder pod that has permanently stopped sequencing for the whole cluster, still holding leadership, reporting a shutdown nobody performed, and leaving no line in its own log for the on-call engineer to find.

findings.summary: A STALE COMMENT BLOCK THAT CONTRADICTS THE ONE TWO LINES ABOVE IT AND DESCRIBES A TEST THAT DOES NOT EXIST. Lines 308-323 state that the enqueue/close atomicity is NOT pinned by any test, that the seam was DELETED from production, and that the property was probed by review instead. Lines 326-335 -- an earlier draft of the same note, left in place -- close with "The deterministic test above pins the same property every run, by parking a caller at the enqueue seam until `close` has fully returned." No test in the file parks a caller at an enqueue seam, the seam is gone from `BatchingSequencer`, and the block immediately above says so. The two blocks also duplicate each other's content (both recount the 8-caller stress test and its 2-of-8 detection rate).
findings.failure_scenario: A future reader -- or a future round of this same review -- reaches line 333 and believes the enqueue/close race is covered by a deterministic test, so a change to `submit`'s `synchronized (lifecycle)` block looks safe to make and the suite will stay green either way. That is exactly the belief lines 308-323 were written to prevent, and the file asserts both propositions at once. Delete lines 326-335; 308-323 already says everything true in them.
